summary.text: A liquid is a state of matter with a definite volume but no fixed shape, so it adapts to the shape of its container.
Its particles are held by bonds of intermediate strength, which let them move around one another while staying closely packed.
Liquids are nearly incompressible, so a pressure change at one point reaches every other part undiminished, which suits them to transmitting hydraulic power.

facts.label: Liquid elements
facts.value: Only mercury and bromine are liquid at standard conditions

facts.label: How common
facts.value: The least common state of matter in the known universe

facts.label: Squeezing water
facts.value: Water compresses by only 46.4 parts per million per bar

facts.label: Helium exception
facts.value: Liquid helium does not become solid even at absolute zero

items.prompt: A mechanic presses the brake pedal and pushes on fluid in a sealed line. What happens to that push at the far end of the line?

options.label: It fades along the way, because the fluid squeezes down to soak it up
It arrives almost undiminished, because little energy goes into squeezing the fluid
It reaches only the nearest part of the fluid and stops there
It doubles, because the fluid stores the push and releases it

items.explain: Liquids barely compress, so a pressure change at one point passes to every other part of the liquid with very little energy lost.

items.prompt: You pour juice from a tall narrow glass into a wide bowl. What happens to the juice?

options.label: It keeps the tall narrow shape it had in the glass
It shrinks to fit the bowl, then expands back later
The amount stays the same, but it spreads to match the bowl
It stays the same shape and the amount drops as it spreads

items.explain: A liquid has a definite volume but no fixed shape, so it adapts to the container it is in.

items.prompt: A student cools carbon dioxide gas at ordinary air pressure, hoping to collect a puddle of it. What does she get instead?

options.label: A thick puddle that boils away the moment it forms
A puddle, because every gas turns liquid when cooled
A cloud that never changes, however cold it gets
A solid, because it skips the liquid stage at that pressure

items.explain: Not every gas can be liquefied at atmospheric pressure. Carbon dioxide solidifies directly and only becomes a liquid at pressures above 5.1 atm.

items.prompt: You heat a pot of water on the stove. What happens to the water molecules as it warms?

options.label: They vibrate harder and drift farther apart
They slow down and pack closer together
They lock into fixed positions as they gain energy
They stay the same, and only the pot gets hotter

items.explain: As temperature rises, molecules in a liquid vibrate more intensely, and the distances between them grow.

items.prompt: A boat propeller spins hard and, over time, its metal gets pitted. What damages it?

options.label: Tiny solid crystals that freeze out of the water and scrape it
Bubbles that form in low-pressure spots, then collapse with strong local force
Water pressing evenly on every side until the metal gives
Dissolved gases that burn the metal as the water heats up

items.explain: Liquid pulled apart in low pressure forms bubbles, which collapse in high-pressure areas and erode nearby solid surfaces.

items.prompt: Water is abundant on Earth. Why are liquids still the rarest state of matter in the universe?

options.label: Water is the only substance that can ever be a liquid
Most of the universe is solid rock, which leaves little room for liquid
They need a fairly narrow range of temperature and pressure to exist
Liquids quickly turn to plasma in space

items.explain: Most known matter is gas or plasma, and liquids need a relatively narrow temperature and pressure range.
